ghost.sample:
Zog was a small dragon. Zog lives behind the moon. Zog eats clouds, and clouds are his only food.

One day, Zog saw a little bird near the moon. The bird was sad. Its nest was on a high rock. "I can't reach it," said the bird. Zog felt kind. He ate clouds as he flew down. He held the nest with his tail and set it near a tree. The bird flew in and felt safe. "Thank you, Zog!" said the bird. Then they played in the soft sky. Zog ate more clouds. The bird sang a sweet song. At night, Zog went home behind the moon. He was glad to help his new friend. The moon shone bright. The wind was soft and warm. The bird gave Zog a shiny rock to keep.

Sisi is a little cloud. Sisi lives in the sky. Sisi likes to sing songs.

One sunny day, Sisi saw a small bird near a tall tree. The bird looked sad. It had lost its song. Sisi flew close, but Sisi stayed in the sky. "I can sing with you," said Sisi. The bird smiled. It listened as Sisi sang a soft song. Then the bird tried. Its voice was small, but it was sweet. More birds came from the tree. They all sang together. The sun came out, and the birds felt happy. Sisi felt happy too. Sisi sang one more song for them. The birds waved their wings and said, "Thank you, Sisi." Sisi waved back. The sky was bright, and all the birds sang on.

Sisi is a little cloud. Sisi lives in the sky. Sisi likes to sing songs. One day, Sisi saw a bird near a tree. The bird was sad. "My nest is wet," said the bird. Sisi felt sorry for her friend. Sisi sang a soft song. The sun came out, and the rain went away. The bird took dry sticks to the tree. Sisi watched from the sky. Soon, the bird made a new nest. "Come and see," said the bird. Sisi smiled. The nest was safe and warm. The bird sat in it and sang too. Sisi sang with her friend. They sang as the sun went down. The sky was pink. The bird felt happy. Sisi felt happy too. They were glad to be friends.

Pip is a tiny robot. Pip loves red apples. Pip sleeps in a teapot. Pip lived near a big garden with a bird named Tim. One wet day, Tim felt sad. His nest was on the ground, and rain fell on it. Pip saw the nest and wanted to help his friend. Pip got a box and put the nest inside it. Tim flew near Pip and sang a happy song. Pip smiled, but the box was wet too. Then Pip found a dry place under a big tree. Tim moved his nest there and felt safe. The rain stopped. The sun came out. Tim gave Pip a warm hug. Pip went home and slept in his teapot. He dreamed of red apples and his good friend.

guide.question: What can I do here?
guide.answer: You can teach a tiny mind, watch it grow, look inside it, see and swap what it is thinking, or hunt for a hidden fact. Minds load by themselves, and the button at the top right switches to expert view with every tab and a files page.
problems: Correctly names the five activities, but adds extra UI guidance not asked for.
'button at the top right switches to expert view with every tab and a files page' is unnecessary and slightly off-status for this front-door answer.
'Minds load by themselves' is extra information not needed for this question.

guide.question: What can I do here?

problems: Good brief list of the five front-door activities, but it misses the detail that in 'see what a mind is thinking' you can also swap a thought.

guide.question: How do I get stories for my character?
guide.answer:
Make sure your character has a name, what kind of thing it is, and two special things. Then use “write 8 stories”; it needs an API key, unless you’re using built-in Claude in a claude.ai artifact, or you can paste in your own stories. Aim for about sixty stories.

DO: SHOW writer

guide.question: How do I get stories for my character?
guide.answer: Fill in your character first, with the name, what kind of thing it is, and the two special things. Then use write eight stories if you have an API key or built-in Claude, or paste your own stories, and aim for about sixty stories in all.

guide.question: Why do some stories get turned away?
guide.answer: Every story is checked against fixed rules: it must be one hundred to one hundred eighty words, have no sentence longer than twenty words, and use familiar words, though the character’s own words are always allowed. It must keep the character’s name, kind, and both special things exactly as written; if a story has only a few unfamiliar words, the ghostwriter gets one chance to repair it.
problems: Adds unsupported details not in the required answer, like 'the character’s own words are always allowed' and 'the ghostwriter gets one chance to repair it.'

Says 'name, kind, and both special things' exactly as written, but the current editor status does not show a kind. The required rule says to keep name, kind, and both special things word for word, but the reply should stay grounded in what is shown on the page.

guide.question: Why do some stories get turned away?
guide.answer:
Some stories are turned away because the app checks every one against fixed rules. A story must be long enough, but not too long, every sentence must stay short, it must use words the tiny mind has met before, and it must keep the character facts exactly the same word for word.

DO: SHOW writer

guide.question: How about farther than the next word?
guide.answer: That’s what thinking ahead shows: the gold words the mind is already planning for later in the story. In layer by layer, pick a piece and press the button to see them in the gold column.

guide.question: How about farther than the next word?
guide.answer: Yes, this mind has thinking ahead. In layer by layer, pick a layer and read the gold column to see what it is already leaning toward farther on in the story, not just the next word.

guide.question: How can I tell if one part of the mind really matters?
guide.answer: Attention patterns and neuron activity are clues, but they don’t prove a part matters. In the switch-off lab, turn off a head or neuron and compare how the story continues with the normal mind and with that part switched off.

guide.question: How can I tell if one part of the mind really matters?
guide.answer: The strongest test is switch-off lab: if the story changes a lot when one head or neuron is muted, that part really matters more than a pretty pattern in attention or layer by layer. Attention and contrast can hint, but ablation is the arbiter.
issues: uses "ablation" instead of the page's "switch off"

guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer:
Attention gives clues about which parts may matter, but it doesn’t show whether they help cause the answer. Switching a part off tests its contribution, though it can’t prove the fact lives in just one place. First, press the probe to ask the mind.  
DO: SHOW probe

guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer: Looking at attention gives clues about where the model is reading, but switch-off tests show what actually changes the answer, so they tell you causal contribution. The clue is that attention can point to a part without proving it is the one storing the fact, and the choir can still sing the song with many voices.
